source_text: Edam jam nunc ego ipsa negotia christianae factionis, ut qui mala refutaverim, bona ostendam. Corpus sumus de conscientia religionis et disciplinae divinitate et spei foedere. Coimus in coetum et congregationem, ut ad Deum, quasi manu facta, precationibus ambiamus. Haec vis Deo grata est. Oramus etiam pro imperatoribus, pro ministeriis eorum ac potestatibus, pro statu seculi, pro rerum quiete, pro mora finis. Cogimur ad litterarum divinarum commemorationem, si quid praesentium temporum qualitas aut praemonere cogit aut recognoscere. Certe fidem sanctis vocibus pascimus, spem erigimus, fiduciam figimus, disciplinam praeceptorum nihilominus in compulsationibus densamus; ibidem etiam exhortationnes, castigationnes et censura divina. Nam et judicatur magno cum pondere, ut apud certos de Dei conspectu, summumque futuri judicii praejudicium est, si quis ita deliquerit, ut a communicatione orationis et conventus et omnis sancti commercii relegetur, Praesident probati quique seniores, honorem istum non pretio sed testimonio adepti; neque enim pretio ulla res Dei constat. Etiam si quod arcae genus est, non de honoraria summa, quasi redemptae religionis congregatur; modicam unusquisque stipem menstrua die, vel quum velit, et si modo velit et si modo possit, apponit: nam nemo compellitur, sed sponte confert. Haec quasi deposita pietatis sunt. Nam inde non epulis nec potaculis, nec ingratis voratrinis dispensatur, sed egenis alendis humandisque, et pueris ac puellis re ac parentibus destitutis, jamque domesticis senibus, item naufragis, et si qui in metallis, et si qui in insulis, vel in custodiis, duntaxat ex caussa Dei sectae alumni confessionis suae fiunt. Sed ejusmodi vel maxime dilectionis operatio notam nobis inurit penes quosdam. Vide, inquiunt, ut invicem se diligant: ipsi enim invicem oderunt; et ut pro alterutro mori sint parati: ipsi enim ad occidendum alterutrum paratiores erunt. Sed et quod fratrum appellatione censemur, non alias, opinor, infamant, quam quod apud ipsos omne sanguinis nomen de affectatione simulatum est. Fratres autem etiam vestri sumus, jure naturae matris unius, etsi vos parum homines, quia mali fratres. At quanto dignius fratres et dicuntur et habentur, qui unum patrem Deum agnoverunt, qui unum Spiritum biberunt sanctitatis, qui de uno utero ignorantiae ejusdem ad unam lucem expaverunt veritatis. Sed eo fortasse minus legitimi existimamur, quia nulla de nostra fraternitate tragoedia exclamat, vel quia ex substantia familiari fratres sumus, quae penes vos fere dirimit fraternitatem. Itaque qui animo animaque miscemur, nihil de rei communicatione dubitamus. Omnia indiscreta sunt apud nos, praeter uxores: in isto loco consortium solvimus, in quo solo caeteri homines consortium exercent, qui non amicorum solummodo matrimonia usurpant, sed et sua amicis patientissime subministrant, ex illa, credo, majorum et sapientissimorum disciplina, Graeci Socratis et Romani Catonis, qui uxores suas amicis communicaverunt, quas in matrimonium duxerant liberorum caussa et alibi creandorum, nescio quidem an invitas; quid enim de castitate curarent, quam mariti tam facile donaverant? O sapientiae Atticae, o Romanae gravitatis exemplum! Leno est philosophus et censor. Quid ergo mirum, si tanta caritas convivatur? Nam et coenulas nostras, praeterquam sceleris infames, ut prodigas quoque suggillatis. De nobis scilicet Diogenis dictum est: Megarenses obsonant quasi crastina die morituri, aedificant vero quasi nunquam morituri. Sed stipulam quis in alieno oculo facilius perspicit, quam in suo trabem. Tot tribubus et curiis et decuriis ructantibus acescit aër. Saliis coenaturis creditor erit necessarius. Herculanarum decimarum et polluctorum sumptus tabularii supputabant. Apaturiis, Dionysiis, mysteriis Atticis coquorum delectus indicentur. Ad fumum coenae Serapiacae sparteoli excitabuntur. De solo triclinio Christianorum retractatur, Coena nostra de nomine rationem sui ostendit; id vocatur, quod dilectio penes Graecos est. Quantiscumque sumptibus constet, lucrum est pietatis nomine facere sumptum, siquidem inopes quosque refrigerio isto juvamus, non qua penes vos parasiti affectant ad gloriam famulandae libertatis sub auctoramento ventris inter contumelias saginandi, sed qua penes Deum major est contemplatio mediocrium. Si honesta caussa est convivii, reliquum ordinem disciplinae aestimate, qui sit de religionnis officio: nihil vilitatis, nihil immodestiae admittit; non prius discumbitur, quam oratio ad Deum praegustetur; editur quantum esurientes capiunt; bibitur quantum pudicis est utile. Ita saturantur, ut qui meminerint etiam per noctem adorandum Deum sibi esse; ita fabulantur, ut qui sciant dominum audire. Post aquam manualem et lumina, ut quisque de scripturis sanctis vel de proprio ingenio potest provocatur in medium Deo canere hinc probatur quomodo biberit. Oeque oratio convivium dirimit. Inde disceditur non in catervas caesionum neque n classes discursationum, nec in eruptiones lasciviarum, sed ad eamdem curam modestiae et pudicitiae ut qui non tam coenam coenaverint, quam disciplinam. Haec coitio christianorum merito sane illicita, si illicitis pari merito damnanda, [si non dissimilis damnandis,] si quis de ea queritur eo titulo, quo de factionibus querela est. In cujus perniciem aliquando convenimus? Hoc sumus congregati, quod et dispersi; hoc universi, quod et singuli; neminem laedentes, neminem contristantes. Quum probi, quum boni coeunt, quum pii, quum casti congregantur, non est factio dicenda, sed curia.
pass_a_gloss: Now I will discuss the business of the Christian sect, so that after refuting the evil, I may show the good. We are a body of people united by our conscience, religion, and divine discipline, and bound together by the hope of our faith. We gather together as a group and congregation to pray to God with united voices, as if with one voice. This power is pleasing to God. We also pray for the emperors, for their ministers and powers, for the state of the world, for peace, and for the delay of the end. We are compelled to recall the divine writings, whether to warn about or recognize the quality of the present times. Certainly, we nourish our faith with holy voices, we lift up our hope, we establish our trust, and we densify the discipline of the teachings, even in the face of compulsions. We also have exhortations, castigations, and divine censures there. For judgment is made with great weight, as if before the certain gaze of God, and it is a pre-judgment of the final judgment, if someone has delinqued to the point of being excluded from the communion of prayer and gathering and all holy commerce. The proven and elderly preside, having obtained this honor not by price but by testimony, for nothing of God's is bought with a price. Even if there is a kind of treasury, it is not gathered from an honorary sum, as if the religion were being redeemed, but each one contributes a small monthly stipend on a fixed day, or when they wish, and if they wish and are able, for no one is compelled, but they contribute spontaneously. These are like deposits of piety. For from them, we do not dispense for feasts or drinks, nor for useless expenditures, but for feeding and burying the needy, and for children and girls who are orphans and without parents, and also for domestic elderly, and for shipwrecked people, and for those who are in mines, and for those who are in islands, or in prisons, provided they become pupils of the confession of God's sect. But this kind of operation of love marks us with a bad reputation among some. 'Look,' they say, 'how they love one another, for they themselves hate one another, and how they are prepared to die for one another, for they are more prepared to kill one another.' But also because we are counted as brothers, I think they do not defame us in any other way than that among them every name of blood relationship is simulated out of affection. We are also your brothers, by the right of nature, of one mother, although you are not good people, because you are evil brothers. But how much more worthy are those who are called and considered brothers, who have recognized one God as Father, who have drunk one Spirit of sanctity, who have been born from one womb of ignorance into one light of truth. But perhaps we are considered less legitimate because no tragedy of our brotherhood cries out, or because we are brothers from a familial substance, which almost destroys brotherhood among you. Therefore, those who are mixed in soul and spirit do not doubt anything about the sharing of things. All things are shared among us, except for wives. In this matter, we dissolve the partnership, in which alone other people exercise partnership, who not only usurp the marriages of friends but also patiently provide their own wives to friends, following, I believe, the discipline of the great and wisest men, the Greek Socrates and the Roman Cato, who shared their wives with friends, whom they had married for the sake of children and to beget elsewhere, I do not know whether willingly or not, for what do they care about chastity, which husbands have easily given away? Oh, example of Attic wisdom and Roman gravity! The philosopher is a pimp and a censor. What wonder is it, then, if such great love is shared? For even our dinners, except for those infamous for crime, are also criticized as prodigal. It has been said about us, surely, that we feast like those who will die tomorrow, but we build like those who will never die. But who can more easily see a straw in someone else's eye than a beam in their own? The air is filled with the belching of so many tribes and curias and decurias. A necessary creditor will be needed for the expenses of the Salian feasts. The sumptuary expenses of the Herculan tables and pollucts are calculated by the tabularii. The choice of cooks is indicated for the Apaturian, Dionysian, and Attic mysteries. The sparteoli are excited by the smoke of the Serapian dinner. But only the dining room of the Christians is criticized. Our dinner, which is called by its name, shows its own reason; it is called what 'love' is among the Greeks. However large the expenses may be, it is profitable to make an expense in the name of piety, since we help all the needy with this refreshment, not as parasites affect to the glory of serving liberty under the authority of the belly, among the insults of being fattened, but as it is greater in the contemplation of the mediocre before God. If the cause of the dinner is honest, estimate the rest of the order of discipline, which is the office of religion: it does not admit anything vile or immodest; we do not recline at table before prayer to God has been tasted; we eat as much as the hungry can take; we drink as much as is useful for the chaste. Thus, they are satiated, so that they remember to adore God even at night; thus, they converse, so that they know the Lord is listening. After the hand-washing and the lights, each one is provoked to sing to God from the holy scriptures or from their own talent. And thus, the prayer concludes the dinner. From there, they depart, not into crowds of caesions or classes of discussions, nor into outbursts of lasciviousness, but to the same care of modesty and chastity, as if they had not dined, but disciplined themselves. This gathering of Christians is rightly considered illicit, if it is to be condemned with equal merit as illicit, if someone complains about it with the same title as a complaint about factions. Against whose destruction do we ever gather? We are gathered for this, which we are also when dispersed; we are all together, which we are also as individuals; we harm no one, we grieve no one. When the good, the upright, the pious, and the chaste gather, it is not to be called a faction, but a curia.

choices.why: technical term for a gathering of people

pass_b_english: I will now take up the affairs of the Christian sect, so that after refuting the charges against us I may display what is good. We are a body knit together by conscience, religion, divine discipline, and the covenant of our hope. We assemble as a congregation to address God in prayer with united voices, as though with a single voice. This power is pleasing to God. We pray also for the emperors, for their ministers and authorities, for the condition of the world, for peace, and for a delay of the end. We are driven to revisit the divine writings, whether the quality of the present times demands warning or recognition. Surely we feed our faith with holy words, lift up our hope, fix our confidence, and tighten the discipline of the precepts even under compulsion; there we also have exhortations, castigations, and divine censure. For judgment is carried out with great weight, as before the very gaze of God, and it serves as a prejudgment of the final judgment, if anyone has so offended that he is excluded from the communion of prayer, assembly, and all holy intercourse. Approved elders preside, having won this honor not by payment but by testimony; for nothing that belongs to God is purchased with a price. Even if there is a kind of treasury, it is not collected from an honorary sum as though religion were being redeemed; rather each person contributes a small monthly amount on a fixed day, or whenever he wishes, and only if he wishes and is able, for no one is compelled but all give freely. These are, as it were, deposits of piety. For from them nothing is spent on banquets or drinking bouts or useless waste, but on feeding and burying the needy, on orphan boys and girls destitute of property and parents, on aged members of our household, on shipwreck victims, on those in mines, on those exiled to islands, or in custody — provided they have become disciples of the confession of God's sect for that very reason. Yet this very practice of love earns us a bad reputation with some people. 'Look,' they say, 'how they love one another' — while they themselves hate one another; 'and how they are ready to die for one another' — while they themselves are more ready to kill one another. Moreover, they slander us precisely because we are called brothers; I suspect for no other reason than that among them every claim of blood kinship is feigned out of mere affectation. We are your brothers too, by the law of nature from a single mother, even though you are hardly human because you are evil brothers. But how much more worthily are those called and regarded brothers who have acknowledged one God as Father, who have drunk one Spirit of holiness, who have been born from one womb of ignorance into one light of truth. Perhaps we are thought less legitimate because no tragedy cries out over our brotherhood, or because we are brothers by a family substance that among you almost destroys brotherhood. Therefore those who are mingled in soul and spirit entertain no doubt about sharing possessions. All things are common among us except wives. In that one point we dissolve the partnership, which is the only partnership other people practice — people who not only usurp the marriages of friends but even obligingly lend their own wives to friends, following, I suppose, the discipline of the greatest and wisest men, the Greek Socrates and the Roman Cato, who shared with friends the wives they had married for the sake of children and for begetting them elsewhere, I do not know whether the wives were willing; for why would they care about chastity when husbands gave it away so easily? O example of Attic wisdom, O Roman gravity! The philosopher acts as a pimp and a censor. What wonder, then, that such great love is practiced among us? Even our dinners — apart from those infamous for crime — you brand as prodigal. Of us it was said, surely, that we feast as if we would die tomorrow, yet build as if we would never die. But who sees a straw in another's eye more easily than a beam in his own? The air grows sour with the belching of so many tribes, curiae, and decuriae. A necessary creditor will be required for the expenses of the Salian feasts. The accountants calculate the costs of the Herculanean tables and pollucta. The choice of cooks is announced for the Apaturia, the Dionysia, and the Attic mysteries. Spartan broths are stirred up by the smoke of the Serapian dinner. Yet only the Christian dining-room comes under scrutiny. Our dinner, by its very name, shows its rationale: it is called by the Greek word for love. Whatever the cost, it is gain to spend in the name of piety, because we relieve every needy person with this refreshment — not as parasites who fawn for the glory of serving liberty under the belly's authority amid insults and fattening, but as those for whom the contemplation of the moderate is greater before God. If the cause of the dinner is honorable, judge the rest of the order of discipline, which belongs to the office of religion: it admits nothing base, nothing immodest; we do not recline before prayer to God has been tasted; we eat only as much as the hungry can take; we drink only as much as is useful for the chaste. Thus they are satisfied in such a way that they remember they must worship God even through the night; thus they converse as those who know the Lord is listening. After the hand-washing and the lights, each is invited to sing to God from the holy scriptures or from his own gift; and so it is proved how he has drunk. Prayer brings the dinner to an end. From there they depart not into crowds of the lewd, nor into classes of dissolute talk, nor into outbreaks of lasciviousness, but to the same care for modesty and chastity, as those who have not so much dined as disciplined themselves. This gathering of Christians is rightly deemed illicit only if it is to be condemned on the same grounds as illicit gatherings; if anyone complains of it under the same title as a complaint against factions. For whose destruction do we ever assemble? We are gathered for this — which we are also when dispersed; we are a whole — which we are also as individuals; we harm no one, we grieve no one. When the upright, the good, the pious, and the chaste come together, it is not to be called a faction, but a curia.
